q: How many commercial banks were nationalised in the first phase of nationalisation?
explain: Fourteen major commercial banks were nationalised in the first phase, on 19 July 1969.

q: On which date were 14 major commercial banks first nationalised in India?
explain: The first nationalisation took place on 19 July 1969. 15 April 1980 is the date of the second phase.

q: Which deposit criterion was used to pick the 14 banks nationalised on 19 July 1969?
explain: All commercial banks with a deposit base of more than ₹50 crore were nationalised in 1969.

q: How many banks were nationalised in the second phase of nationalisation?
explain: Six banks were nationalised in 1980 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980.

q: When was the second phase of bank nationalisation carried out?
explain: Six more banks were nationalised on 15 April 1980. The first phase was in July 1969.

q: Which of the following Indian banks was never a nationalised bank?
explain: Federal Bank is a private sector bank. Corporation, Vijaya and Oriental Bank of Commerce were nationalised in 1980.

q: Nationalisation of banks aimed at all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Removal of control by a few capitalists
Provision of credit to big industries only
Access of banking to the masses
Encouragement of a new class of entrepreneurs
explain: The aim was wider credit for agriculture, SMEs and exports, not credit for big industries alone.

q: Which of the following banks was nationalised in 1980 and NOT in 1969?
explain: Andhra Bank was among the six banks of 1980. Canara, Union and Indian Bank were nationalised in 1969.

q: Which of these banks was NOT among the 14 banks nationalised in 1969?
explain: Corporation Bank came in the 1980 list. Dena, Syndicate and UCO Bank were nationalised in 1969.

q: Under which Act were six banks nationalised in 1980?
options: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980
Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948
explain: The 1980 nationalisation was carried out under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980. The 1948 Act nationalised RBI itself.

q: What was the stated reason for the second phase of nationalisation in 1980?
options: To give the government more control over credit delivery
To start the Reserve Bank of India
To merge SBI with its associates
explain: The government wanted tighter control over credit delivery. After this phase it controlled about 91 per cent of banking business.

q: After the second phase of nationalisation, the government controlled around what share of banking business in India, according to the syllabus?
explain: After the 1980 phase, about 91 per cent of banking business was under government control.

q: In 1993, which nationalised bank became the first to be merged with another bank?
explain: New Bank of India merged with Punjab National Bank in 1993, the first merger of a nationalised bank.

q: New Bank of India was merged in 1993 with which bank, which traced its roots to Lahore?
explain: Punjab National Bank, whose roots lie in Lahore, absorbed New Bank of India in 1993.

q: After New Bank of India merged with PNB in 1993, how many nationalised banks remained from the 1969 and 1980 lists?
explain: 14 (1969) plus 6 (1980) gave 20; after the 1993 merger the figure was 19.

q: Which of the following was NOT an objective of bank nationalisation?
options: Mobilising national savings for productive use
Extending banking facilities to unbanked rural areas
explain: Nationalisation aimed at social goals such as rural banking and mobilising savings, not at higher private dividends.

q: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of bank nationalisation in India?
options: Inadequate banking facilities in backward states
explain: Nationalisation expanded branches in rural and semi-urban areas. The real limitations were inadequate facilities, lower efficiency and higher costs.

q: Which Act of 1959 led to the creation of eight subsidiaries of the State Bank of India?
options: State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act
explain: Eight subsidiaries were made under the State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959.

q: How many subsidiaries of SBI were made under the SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act of 1959?
explain: The 1959 Act created eight subsidiaries. The number later fell to five after mergers in 1963, 2008 and 2010.

q: In 1963, SBI merged State Bank of Jaipur and State Bank of Bikaner to form which bank?
options: State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur
explain: The Jaipur (founded 1943) and Bikaner (founded 1944) banks were merged into the State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur.

q: In which year did State Bank of Saurashtra merge with SBI?
explain: State Bank of Saurashtra merged in 2008. State Bank of Indore followed in 2010, leaving five associates.

q: After the merger of State Bank of Indore with SBI in 2010, how many associate banks of SBI remained?
explain: With Saurashtra gone in 2008 and Indore in 2010, five associates were left: Hyderabad, Mysore, Patiala, Travancore and Bikaner and Jaipur.

q: Along with the five associate banks, which other bank merged with SBI on 1 April 2017?
explain: Bharatiya Mahila Bank and SBI's five associates merged with SBI on 1 April 2017.

q: Which of the following was NOT an associate bank of SBI merged in 2017?
explain: Bank of Baroda is a separate nationalised bank. Mysore, Patiala and Travancore were SBI associates.

q: Which date is observed as SBI Day?
explain: 1 July is observed as SBI Day. 1 April 2017 was the date of the associate-bank merger and logo change.

q: Until the Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935, which bank performed some central banking functions?
explain: The Imperial Bank of India, now SBI, performed certain central banking functions as well as commercial banking.

q: SBI acts as the agent of RBI in:
options: Places where RBI has no branch of its own
Places where cooperative banks are absent
explain: SBI acts as RBI's agent wherever RBI does not have its own branches.

q: Which statement about Reserve Bank of India is correct?
options: It was set up in 1935 and nationalised on 1 January 1949
It was set up in 1949 and nationalised in 1969
It was set up in 1935 and nationalised in 1980
It was set up in 1955 and nationalised in 1969
explain: RBI began in April 1935 and was nationalised on 1 January 1949 under the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948.

q: Which of the following did the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 provide?
options: No new bank or branch could open without an RBI licence
SBI would handle all government banking
explain: The Act required an RBI licence for new banks and branches and barred two banks from having common directors.

q: The Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) was established in which year to provide long-term finance to industry?
explain: IDBI was set up in 1964 because commercial banks mainly offered short-term finance.

q: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 envisaged which kind of economy?
explain: The resolution envisaged a mixed economy, with greater state involvement in sectors including banking and finance.

q: Which of the following banks was set up after the reforms and was earlier named UTI Bank?
explain: UTI Bank is now known as Axis Bank.

q: On which date was the high-level Committee on the Financial System (CFS) set up?
explain: The CFS was set up on 14 August 1991; its recommendations led to comprehensive reform from 1992-93.

q: The Narasimham Committee-II on banking sector reforms was set up in December of which year?
explain: It was set up in December 1997 and handed over its report in April 1998.

q: Under the 3-tier banking structure suggested after mergers, Tier 1 was to have:
options: A large number of local banks
explain: Tier 1 would have 2 to 3 international banks, Tier 2 would have 8 to 10 national banks and Tier 3 many local banks.

q: How many banks of national orientation were proposed for Tier 2 of the suggested banking structure?
explain: Tier 2 was to have 8 to 10 banks of national orientation.

q: To what level did Narasimham Committee-II suggest raising the capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR)?
explain: The committee suggested a higher CRAR, raised to 10 per cent.

q: Which of the following was NOT a suggestion of Narasimham Committee-II?
options: Depoliticise bank boards under RBI supervision
Strengthen the legal framework for loan recovery
Increase budgetary recapitalisation of public sector banks
explain: The committee said budgetary recapitalisation of PSBs was not viable and should be dropped.

q: Which Act, passed in 2002, strengthened loan recovery in line with a Narasimham Committee-II suggestion?
explain: The government passed the SARFAESI Act in 2002 to strengthen the legal framework for loan recovery.

q: Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank were merged into which bank with effect from 1 April 2019?
explain: Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank merged into Bank of Baroda on 1 April 2019.

q: Which nationalised bank merged into Canara Bank in the 2020 round of public sector bank mergers?
explain: Syndicate Bank merged with Canara Bank on 1 April 2020. Allahabad merged into Indian Bank; Andhra and Corporation into Union Bank.
